name: Clomiphene
lead: Clomiphene citrate (Clomid) is a selective estrogen receptor modulator taken by mouth. The US label indicates it for ovulatory dysfunction in women desiring pregnancy, particularly polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).[1] In men it is used off-label for hypogonadism, where it aims to raise the body's own testosterone and preserve sperm production, in contrast to exogenous testosterone.[2]

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities clomiphene is discussed under labels such as 'tmaxxing' and post-cycle therapy: users describe taking it to boost endogenous testosterone, and compare it with enclomiphene, one of its isomers, which one thread says boosted testosterone more with fewer side effects in a 2024 study.[3][4] Several posters are teenagers asking how to obtain it without a prescription.[5]

A 2022 systematic review of clomiphene in men with hypogonadism included 19 studies, four of them randomised, and assessed hormone levels, symptoms and safety.[2] The label lists ovarian enlargement and vasomotor flushes as the most common adverse events and warns of visual symptoms that are usually reversible but may be irreversible.[1]
infobox: Ovulatory dysfunction in women desiring pregnancy

paras: Women: the US label's indication is ovulatory dysfunction, and PCOS is named among the conditions most likely to respond.[1] Clomiphene was long the first-line drug for ovulation induction in PCOS. A 2014 randomised trial found letrozole superior to clomiphene for live birth in PCOS, and later meta-analyses and a Cochrane review compare the two.[6][7][8][9] Randomised trials have also tested clomiphene with acupuncture and in stair-step protocols.[10][11]

Men: a systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated clomiphene as off-label therapy for male hypogonadism, noting that exogenous testosterone suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and spermatogenesis, which clomiphene is intended to avoid.[2]

Appearance-related use centres on raising testosterone for muscle, body composition and masculine traits, and on recovering natural testosterone after anabolic steroid cycles. On looksmax.org one poster states that clomid is taken after a cycle rather than cycled; another asks whether it could replace injecting testosterone, and a reply says it boosts testosterone but must be taken indefinitely and exogenous testosterone will always be better.[3]

The US label reports ovarian enlargement (13.6%), vasomotor flushes (10.4%), abdominal-pelvic discomfort and nausea among adverse events above 1% in studies of 8,029 patients, and warns of visual disturbances such as blurring or scintillating scotomata that increase with total dose or treatment duration; the label says cases of prolonged disturbance have been reported and they may be irreversible.[1] It is contraindicated in pregnancy; human data do not suggest a higher congenital anomaly risk, but animal studies showed embryo-fetal loss and malformations.[1]
In T Nation threads, men prescribed clomiphene for low testosterone or fertility report variable experiences, including increased libido in some and, in one thread, loss of libido.[13][14][15]

As a SERM, clomiphene blocks oestrogen receptors in the hypothalamus and pituitary, which raises gonadotropin release and, in men, stimulates testicular testosterone production.[2] Enclomiphene is one of its two isomers, studied separately in trials of men with secondary hypogonadism.[16][17][4]

Evidence in women: the 2014 NEJM trial of letrozole versus clomiphene in PCOS,[6] the 2023 meta-analysis,[7] a 2022 Cochrane review,[9] and a 2017 JAMA trial of acupuncture and clomiphene.[10] Evidence in men: the 2022 systematic review of 19 studies (four randomised) in hypogonadism,[2] and registered phase 3 trials of enclomiphene in men with secondary hypogonadism, including studies of 499 and 300 participants.[16][17]
No trials were identified of clomiphene used for cosmetic aims in healthy men or for height in adolescents. Registered work also includes an anti-doping metabolism study of clomiphene.[18]

Looksmax.org threads cover how clomid works and whether it must be cycled, comparisons with enclomiphene for use alongside MK-677 or Anavar post-cycle therapy, and requests from a self-described 15-year-old to buy it without a prescription after parents and a doctor declined.[3][4][5] T Nation users on testosterone therapy or fertility treatment describe starting clomiphene under physician guidance and compare outcomes.[13][14][15][19]

lore.intro: Clomiphene is discussed as a testosterone-boosting alternative to injected testosterone and as post-cycle therapy, with enclomiphene debated as a cleaner option.[3][4]

claims.claim: Clomid raises natural testosterone without injections
claims.believers: Posters say it boosts endogenous testosterone and could serve 'tmaxxing', though others note it has to be taken long term.[3]
claims.experts: A systematic review of 19 studies in hypogonadal men assessed hormone levels and symptoms and describes the use as off-label.[2]

claims.claim: Enclomiphene raises testosterone more than clomiphene with fewer side effects
claims.believers: A poster cites a September 2024 article comparing the two.[4]
claims.experts: Registered phase 3 trials examined enclomiphene in men with secondary hypogonadism; the label for clomiphene lists its own adverse events.[16][17][1]

claims.claim: Clomiphene helps recovery after a steroid cycle
claims.believers: Users take it after a cycle.[3]
claims.experts: No published trial of clomiphene as post-cycle therapy was identified in the sources reviewed.

card.summary: A fertility SERM that men use off-label to lift their own testosterone; some evidence in hypogonadal men, none for looks.
card.note: Label warns of possibly irreversible visual disturbances; male use is off-label.

quick.overview:
Clomiphene (Clomid) is a prescription drug for ovulation induction in women. Men use it off-label to raise their own testosterone, and looksmax.org discusses it for 'tmaxxing' and post-cycle recovery.

A 2022 review covers its use in hypogonadal men; no trials test it for cosmetic goals in healthy people.
quick.mechanism: It blocks oestrogen receptors in the brain's hypothalamus and pituitary, raising gonadotropins and prompting the testes to make more testosterone.
quick.risks: The label lists ovarian enlargement and flushes, plus visual disturbances that may be irreversible. Users report mood and libido changes. Prescription-only; teens asking for it without a prescription appear on forums.
